summary: Tulare County sprawls across nearly 4,840 square miles — larger than the entire state of Connecticut — yet holds fewer than half a million people, which means a population density of just 100 per square mile and a landscape that shifts dramatically from dead-flat San Joaquin Valley farmland in the west to the crest of the southern Sierra Nevada in the east, where Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks sit entirely or partly within county lines. That geographic range is the defining feature: dairy operations and citrus groves dominate the valley floor, while 14,000-foot peaks loom to the east, all under roughly 9.5 hours of daily sunshine and mild average highs around 67°F (though valley summers regularly push well past 100°F, and tule fog can blank out winter mornings for weeks). Agriculture and food processing — not tech, not tourism — anchor the economy, making this one of the top-producing agricultural counties in the nation, with major employers in dairy, cattle, and tree fruit. A median home value of $303,000 against a median household income near $69,500 yields a price-to-income ratio around 4.4, meaningfully more accessible than coastal California, though a poverty rate of 17.8% signals that affordability and prosperity are not the same thing. Tulare County is a place where the distance between your grocery store and a giant sequoia grove can be measured in a single hour's drive — but so can the distance between your house and the nearest urban amenity you might take for granted elsewhere.
